bp: The real object in this tutorial is a web system that no longer only returns pages or writes answers. It acts: a language model can choose what text to generate, which content to show, which recommendation strategy to try, which other agent to coordinate with, and how to adjust after users or partner agents respond. That turns the web into a continuing decision environment. A fixed language model is like a clerk with a script: useful for familiar requests, but weak when the right move depends on live feedback. The tutorial argues that multi-armed bandits fit this setting because they treat each possible action as an option whose value is partly unknown. The need comes before the method: agentic language systems must keep serving users while learning which choices work. They cannot pause the world to test every possible response, content item, or interaction style.
wh: The hard part is that every action has two jobs at once. It should be useful now, and it should teach the system something useful for later. If an agent always picks the response, article, tool path, or recommendation style that has worked best so far, it may miss a better option that has not yet had enough trials. If it experiments too freely, real users receive worse answers or irrelevant content while the system learns. The abstract also places the problem in a networked multi-agent setting, where one agent's behavior can affect another agent's response. That makes feedback less clean than a laboratory label. A reward may reflect the generated text, the user's taste, another agent's strategy, timing, or a platform goal. The system must learn under uncertainty while staying fast enough for web scale and stable enough for autonomous operation.
naive: A smart beginner would choose a few rules by hand: always use the highest-rated generation style, always recommend the category with the most clicks, or let each language-model agent follow the same fixed prompt and update it occasionally from aggregate results. This fails because early evidence can be misleading. The first winning option may simply have been shown to easier users or tried at a lucky time. A rule also wastes the chance to learn from uncertain alternatives. In personalized content and recommendation, different users may reward different choices, so one global winner can become a trap. In multi-agent dialogue, a fixed behavior can stop adapting when other agents change.
ap: The central move is to put a small decision engine around the language model. Instead of treating generation or recommendation as one fixed path, the system lists possible actions as arms: alternative text-generation choices, content-selection policies, interaction strategies, or recommendation moves. After choosing one, it observes a reward, meaning some measurable sign that the choice helped, such as better interaction quality, stronger content fit, or a successful recommendation outcome. The agent then updates its belief about that option while keeping some room to test other options. The tutorial covers familiar bandit strategies such as epsilon-greedy, UCB, and Thompson Sampling. In plain terms, these are different ways to decide when to trust the current favorite and when to try an uncertain option because the missing knowledge may be worth the temporary risk.
mech: The mechanism starts with a situation: a user request, a content feed moment, a dialogue turn between agents, or a recommendation opportunity. The language model or agentic platform has a set of candidate moves. Each candidate is treated as an arm, not because it is literally a slot-machine handle, but because pulling it means trying that action and receiving feedback afterward. The system chooses an arm using an exploration policy. In epsilon-greedy, most choices follow the currently best-known arm, while a small share deliberately tests another arm. In UCB, an arm gets credit both for high observed reward and for uncertainty, so options with little evidence can still be tried. In Thompson Sampling, the system samples from its current belief about each arm and lets uncertainty naturally produce experiments. After the action, the system records a reward signal. The reward design is crucial: it must translate messy outcomes such as dialogue coordination, content relevance, or recommendation success into a number or comparable signal. The bandit updater then changes the estimated value of the chosen arm. Over many interactions, weak arms are chosen less often, useful arms are chosen more often, and uncertain arms still receive enough trials to avoid premature lock-in. The output is not just text; it is an adaptive policy for future web actions.
math: The main mathematical idea is decision-making under uncertainty. A multi-armed bandit is a repeated-choice problem where each option has an unknown payoff, and the learner only observes the payoff of the option it actually tried. That limited feedback matters here because an agent does not know what would have happened if it had generated a different response or shown a different item. Probability enters as measured belief: the system estimates how likely each action is to produce useful feedback based on past trials, while admitting that thin evidence should not be treated as certainty. The exploration-exploitation trade-off is the central pressure. Exploitation means using the option that currently looks best; exploration means spending some decisions to learn about options whose value is still unclear. UCB adds an uncertainty bonus, which is a way of saying that an option with few observations deserves a chance before being dismissed. Thompson Sampling turns uncertain belief into randomized choice, so less-certain options are tried in proportion to how plausible their success still is. Optimization, in this paper's sense, means repeatedly adjusting the action-choice rule to improve the reward signal. The risk is that the reward number compresses many human and platform goals into one target.
dots: This tutorial sits at the crossing of several recurring conference ideas. It belongs with LLM agents and tool-use work because the language model is being treated as a worker that chooses actions, coordinates with other agents, and adapts from outcomes rather than only producing one answer. It belongs with recommender-systems work because content selection and recommendation are short-listing problems: many possible items or strategies compete for a small amount of user attention. It belongs with reinforcement-learning work because the system acts, observes feedback, and changes future behavior, although the bandit setting is narrower because it focuses on repeated choices with limited feedback rather than full long-horizon planning. It also connects to probability and ranking. Probability keeps uncertainty visible when evidence is partial, while ranking appears whenever arms are ordered by expected usefulness. The common field-level problem is controlled attention: decide what to try next when acting teaches the system but can also cost users, money, time, or trust.
ww: The approach should help because agentic web systems contain repeated decision points with feedback. A language model does not have to solve every future case from first principles if past interactions reveal that certain generation choices, content policies, or recommendation strategies often work in similar settings. Bandits improve on the naive fixed rule by refusing to confuse current evidence with final truth. An option that has done well receives more use, so the system benefits from what it has learned. An option that has little evidence can still be tested, so the system can discover better behavior after user needs, available content, or other agents change. This is especially natural for web-scale systems, where the same kind of choice recurs many times and small updates can accumulate into better routing of attention. The mechanism also fits decentralized agentic settings because each agent can adapt from its own observed rewards without requiring a single complete model of the whole web. The benefit depends on feedback being frequent and meaningful enough to guide learning.
po: The payoff is an agentic language platform that can keep adapting instead of relying only on fixed prompts or offline training. The tutorial's examples point to three capabilities: coordinating multi-agent dialogue, dynamically curating personalized content, and improving recommendation strategies. In each case, the bandit layer gives the system a disciplined way to try alternatives, learn from response signals, and gradually favor actions that work better in practice. The result is not a guarantee of perfect autonomy; it is a practical control loop for systems that must make many small web decisions while evidence is still incomplete.
limits: Several assumptions must hold. The system needs a reward signal that truly reflects the desired outcome; clicks, engagement, or short-term satisfaction can mislead if they ignore quality, safety, diversity, or long-term trust. The set of arms must be defined well enough that useful alternatives are available to test. Feedback must arrive often enough for learning, and past interactions must remain relevant as users, content, and other agents change. The abstract names case studies but does not prove which reward designs, exploration policies, or scaling choices are safest across all agentic web deployments.
